overview: This bill, the Pipeline Security Act, writes into law that the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), part of the Department of Homeland Security, is responsible for protecting oil and gas pipelines from cyberattacks, terrorism and other security threats, working with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as needed. The TSA would keep pipeline security guidelines up to date in line with federal cybersecurity standards, issue security directives or regulations when needed, share threat information with industry and governments, rank risks, and inspect pipeline operators' security plans and facilities. Within 180 days the TSA would have to produce a staffing plan, including how to build its cybersecurity expertise, and it would report to Congress at least every two years. The Government Accountability Office, Congress's watchdog, would review how the law is carried out. On November 12, 2025, the House Homeland Security Committee reported it and it was placed on the House calendar for a floor vote.
for: Supporters say pipelines are vital to the nation's energy supply and a clear legal assignment of security duties to the TSA, plus more cyber expertise, would make them harder to attack.
against: Critics say the bill leaves pipeline cybersecurity with an agency best known for airport screening and gives it broad power to issue directives that could burden operators.
